concept.name: Concentration risk
concept.definition: The risk arising from an uneven distribution of exposures — to a single counterparty or name (name concentration) or to a sector, region, or product (sectoral concentration) — such that one adverse event can produce losses large enough to threaten the portfolio or institution.
concept.intuition: Concentration is the opposite of diversification: the more eggs in one basket, the more one dropped basket costs.
concept.mechanics: Monitored through concentration ratios (the share of the portfolio in the largest exposures) and indices such as the Herfindahl index; banks set internal limits and regulators attach higher capital charges to concentrated books. In trading, the analogues are per-position and per-sector exposure caps.
concept.formula: Single-name concentration ratio = exposure_i / total portfolio; portfolio level: Herfindahl index H = sum_i s_i^2, where s_i are exposure shares.
concept.failure_modes: Concentration metrics treat categories as independent; in crises, apparently separate names correlate through shared factors or funding channels, so measured concentration understates true common exposure. Ratio-based limits also ignore tail severity within the concentrated bucket.
concept.misconceptions: Concentration risk is not eliminated by holding many small positions in the same theme — correlated positions are one bet — and high conviction does not repeal the arithmetic of undiversified downside.
concept.example: A portfolio of 10 loans where one loan is half the book has a single-name concentration ratio of 50% and a Herfindahl index of about 0.27, versus 0.10 for an equally sized book.
